extracted.intended_audience: media professionals and general readers interested in journalism and media-industry accountability
extracted.subtask_description: News reporting about a journalistic retraction and the ethical/accuracy failures that prompted it. Focuses on why an article was corrected and ultimately retracted and what that implies about editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: “New information emerged that raised serious concerns about its accuracy,” leading to corrections and ultimately retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify core factual claims before publication; examples in the article include misstated rink sizes, the extent of an injury, and the location of a family. Multiple factual errors can lead editors to lose confidence in an article's veracity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and trustworthiness of the author
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors stated: “We cannot attest to the trustworthiness and credibility of the author, and therefore we cannot attest to the veracity of the article.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author’s credibility is a criterion for whether an outlet can stand behind a piece; serious doubts about an author's honesty or integrity can justify retraction even if some facts might be correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty with fact-checkers / editors
rubrics_metrics.description: The author “admitted to being ‘complicit’ in deceiving the magazine's fact-checkers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately misleading fact-checkers or editors is unacceptable and is a clear ground for retraction or other remedial editorial action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and verification of anonymous sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atlantic’s note cited deception about a section concerning a person referred to as 'Sloane' (including a false claim that she had a son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When anonymity is used, outlets must still verify attributable facts; fabricating or suggesting false personal details to preserve anonymity undermines verifiability and is unethical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections policy and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece had an initial correction (Oct. 22) and additional corrections before the retraction; the outlet provided a link to a PDF version of the piece as it appears in print “to maintain transparency.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish timely corrections when errors are found; if errors accumulate or credibility is compromised, consider retraction. Provide transparent editor’s notes and, where appropriate, access to the original or corrected text for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial decision to retract when veracity cannot be attested
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors decided: “We have decided to retract this article. We cannot attest to the trustworthiness and credibility of the author, and therefore we cannot attest to the veracity of the article.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction is appropriate when editorial leadership determines they cannot vouch for the truthfulness of a piece, particularly when author integrity or key facts are in serious doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of specific factual details (measurements, injuries, locations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article cites concrete misstatements such as a claim about “Olympic size” hockey rinks that misstated the size, and errors about the extent of an injury and a family's location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-check precise, verifiable details (dimensions, dates, locations, medical information); such granular errors weaken overall credibility and are often easier to detect and correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of author’s past conduct when assessing credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece notes Barrett was accused of plagiarism in the 1990s (when she went by Ruth Shalit), and that context is part of the broader story of credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author’s prior history of ethical lapses (e.g., past plagiarism) can and should factor into editorial vetting and the threshold for remedial actions such as corrections or retraction.
